items.summary: Research data and software supporting the derivation and literature reconstruction of relative-sensitivity expressions in inverse multiple linear regression luminescence thermometry. Includes executable Excel calculations for 22 model-temperature cases from seven papers, literature classification and equation-lineage evidence, numerical reconstruction code, analytical figure data, editable figure sources, and preserved Lean 4 and AXLE verification records. Effective sensitivities are conditional on the stated reference noise model and recovered local gain. Unresolved reconstruction discrepancies and the limited scope of formal verification are documented.
items.title: Data and software for "A reciprocal-derivative error inflates relative sensitivity in multivariate luminescence thermometry"

items.summary: This record contains the complete R and Python code and supporting documentation for the independent sensitivity reanalysis associated with the manuscript “Swab-based stool collection largely preserves gut microbiome structure with small device-dependent effects: an intra-individual evaluation of sampling devices and processing conditions.” The archive includes scripts to reconstruct and validate anonymous sample metadata from the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) run report and FASTQ filenames; perform preliminary read-quality and paired-read overlap assessments; process forward (R1) and reverse (R2) reads separately using DADA2; infer ASVs; assign taxonomy using the SILVA SSU NR99 release 138.2 training set; construct phylogenetic trees; evaluate sequencing-depth dependence; calculate standardized alpha- and beta-diversity metrics, including Faith’s phylogenetic diversity, weighted UniFrac, and Bray–Curtis dissimilarity; compare the R1 and R2 results; assess sensitivity to rarefaction depth and unusually long terminal branches; and generate the corresponding tables and figures. The archive also contains a complete execution guide, software dependencies and versions, random seeds, original R session information, reference-database details, and file-integrity checksums. Sample metadata and analytical outputs are generated locally by the documented workflow and are not distributed as precomputed files. Raw paired-end sequencing data are publicly available from the European Nucleotide Archive under accession PRJEB107991. The DADA2-formatted SILVA 138.2 taxonomic training set is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14169026 . The independent ASV analyses complement, but do not reproduce or replace, the proprietary MicrobAT® workflow used for the primary OTU-based analysis. MicrobAT® algorithms, OTU-assignment parameters, and the release of its embedded reference database were not disclosed by the software provider. Accordingly, this archive supports reproducibility of the independent R1/R2 ASV sensitivity analyses and downstream analyses of the published MicrobAT® outputs, but not reconstruction of the proprietary MicrobAT®-generated OTU and taxonomic profiles. This version supersedes the earlier R-only archive by adding the Python utilities, complete operational documentation, software-environment records, random seeds, integrity checks, and portable figure-generation scripts.
items.title: Reproducibility code for: Swab-based stool collection largely preserves gut microbiome structure with small device-dependent effects

items.summary: Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. Every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_TailWatch . Interactive studio: https://tailwatch.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1, descending frame 124D_04854_171313 (2016-2018), redistributed under the Copernicus free-and-open licence with LiCSBAS attribution (Morishita et al. 2020); provenance in data/derived/tw-real-cf.provenance.json.
items.title: TailWatch: An InSAR Deformation-Monitoring and Inverse-Velocity Failure-Forecasting Studio, on Synthetic Sentinel-1 and Real Campi Flegrei

items.summary: Benchmark package accompanying the manuscript “Failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems: residual-error decoupling, an attainable-accuracy bound and an identifiability benchmark”. The package contains: the exact solution of the beam–two-mass moving-load benchmark and the modal and RK4 reference baselines on the same grid; the training campaign with random seeds, network configurations, collocation densities, training budgets, measured wall-clock times, residuals and relative-L2 errors for every run; the inverse-problem (speed and load-amplitude) campaign with its identifiability verdict; the weights of the reference physics-informed network; and the scripts that regenerate every figure, table and number of the paper. It supports two results of the paper: the residual–error decoupling for moving singular sources, and the attainable-accuracy bound obtained by fitting the same architecture to the exact solution. All runs are seeded, so the accuracy–cost comparison reported in the paper can be re-derived without retraining.

items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across diverse applications, raising critical questions for governance, accountability, and data provenance. Understanding which training data most influenced a model's output remains a fundamental open problem. We address this challenge through training data attribution (TDA) for auto-regressive LLMs by expanding upon the inverse formulation: How would training data be affected if the model had seen the generated output during training? Our method perturbs the base model using bidirectional gradient optimization (gradient ascent and descent) on a generated text sample and measures the resulting change in loss across training samples. Our framework supports attribution at arbitrary data granularity, enabling both factual and stylistic attribution. We evaluate our method against baselines on pretrained models with known datasets, and show that it outperforms previous work on influence metrics, thereby enhancing model interpretability, an essential requirement for accountable AI systems.
items.title: Data Attribution in Large Language Models via Bidirectional Gradient Optimization

items.summary: FPGA-Accelerated Sub-Microsecond Union-Find Decoding for Real-Time Surface-Code Quantum Memory Architecture manuscript. Latency, power, and resource figures are design estimates unless otherwise marked as measured. Related FPGA Union-Find implementations (Helios / Collision Clustering) are cited for comparison. Abstract Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires continuous decoding of stabilizer syndromes within cycle times that, for superconducting processors, are often 200 ns–1 μs. Host-processor decoders are subject to operating-system jitter, DMA overhead, and memory-hierarchy latency, which make deterministic sub-microsecond service difficult. This paper describes a fully pipelined FPGA architecture for a Union-Find decoder aimed at surface-code quantum memory. The pipeline integrates Aurora-based syndrome acquisition, streaming defect extraction, a path-halving Union-Find engine with hazard forwarding, localized peeling, and dual-port Pauli-frame updates. All latency-critical state is on-chip (BRAM, UltraRAM, distributed RAM). At a target clock of 400 MHz the design estimate for end-to-end latency is 170–390 ns below threshold, with a conservative worst-case bound near 500 ns—inside a 1 μs cycle. Memory for a decoding window scales as O(d³) with the space-time graph, not as O(d³) measurements per cycle. Power is estimated at 3–6 W per logical patch at the FPGA, which remains at room temperature. The contribution is a single deterministic pipeline that does not require a host CPU in the inner loop. It is an architecture and resource plan; it does not replace measured implementations such as Helios. Keywords: surface code; quantum error correction; Union-Find decoder; FPGA; real-time decoding; Pauli frame; clock gating. 1. Introduction Surface-code fault tolerance proceeds by repeated stabilizer measurement and classical decoding of the syndrome stream [1], [9], [10]. Superconducting cycle times commonly fall in T_cycle ~ 200 ns–1 μs [13]. Software decoders on CPUs or GPUs introduce scheduling jitter, DMA cost, cache misses, and synchronization [14]–[16]. Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) is accurate but worst-case cubic in the number of defects and heavy for large distance [17], [18]. The Union-Find decoder of Delfosse and Nickerson is almost-linear and close to MWPM in accuracy, which makes it a natural hardware target [3]. FPGA and ASIC decoders have already shown that real-time surface-code decoding is possible. Das et al. gave a Union-Find micro-architecture; Liyanage et al. (Helios) implemented distributed Union-Find on a VCU129 up to d = 21 with mean times of order 10 ns per round under phenomenological noise, and a resource-optimized d = 51 point near 544 ns per round [14], [15]. Collision Clustering, another Union-Find variant, has been mapped to FPGA and ASIC with sub-microsecond times at large patch size [16]. The present manuscript specifies a single-tile, fully streaming pipeline—acquisition through Pauli frame—with explicit memory equations, banked Find ports, path-halving (not recursive compression), clock-enable power control, and a latency budget written against T_cycle = 1 μs. It is intended as a self-contained hardware architecture that can be implemented or compared against those measured designs. 2. System Architecture The decoder is a fixed-depth pipeline. Stages are registered and advance on the same clock. After fill, a new syndrome frame can be accepted every cycle from the control layer; variable work inside Union-Find is bounded by a worst-case iteration budget, not by a host thread. Stages: •     Syndrome acquisition and deserialization (Aurora 64B/66B over GTY). •     Defect extraction unit (DEU): frame-to-frame XOR and sparse packing. •     Pipelined Union-Find engine: growth, union, path-halving find, boundary test. •     Localized peeling
items.title: FPGA-Accelerated Sub-Microsecond Union-Find Decoding for Real-Time Surface-Code Quantum Memory

items.summary: # FaultNet This archive contains the trained models, example earthquake catalog, and Jupyter notebook used to apply **FaultNet**, a deep-learning framework for reconstructing three-dimensional fault structures from earthquake hypocenters. FaultNet uses two PointNet++-based models followed by agglomerative clustering and fault surface reconstruction by radial basis function. The first model, denoising model, identifies fault-related earthquakes and removes background seismicity. The second model, feature learning model, maps the remaining earthquakes into an embedding space in which earthquakes associated with the same fault have similar representations. Pairwise similarities estimated from overlapping spatial windows are combined into a global distance matrix and used for clustering. The resulting earthquake clusters can then be reconstructed as continuous three-dimensional fault surfaces using radial basis function (RBF) interpolation. ## Files and directories - `apply_FaultNet.ipynb`     Main notebook demonstrating the complete FaultNet inference workflow, including:   1. loading the trained models;   2. loading and visualizing an earthquake catalog;   3. selecting a sliding-window size;   4. identifying fault-related earthquakes;   5. learning feature embedding and agglomerative clustering;   6. reconstructing fault surfaces using RBF interpolation; and   7. evaluating and visualizing the reconstructed surfaces. - `example_catalog.npy`   Example earthquake catalog used in the notebook. The array has shape `(N, 5)`, with columns:   `x, y, z, horizontal_location_error, vertical_location_error`.   Spatial coordinates and location uncertainties should use consistent distance units (km in the provided example).   Users can replace it with another earthquake catalog following the same format. Coordinates and uncertainties should be expressed in a consistent Cartesian coordinate system and distance unit. - `example_prediction.npy`     Example FaultNet clustering output corresponding to `example_catalog.npy`. It contains one integer label per earthquake. A label of `-1` denotes background seismicity or clusters excluded by the minimum-size criterion (50 events); non-negative integers identify reconstructed fault clusters. - `model_I_denoising/`     Trained denoising model for distinguishing fault-related earthquakes from background seismicity. The trained weights used by the notebook are stored in `checkpoints/best_model.pth`. - `model_II_feature_learning/`     Trained feature learning model for generating 8-dimensional embedding representations of fault-related earthquakes. The trained weights used by the notebook are stored in `checkpoints/best_model.pth`. - `Pointnet_Pointnet2_pytorchmaster/`     PointNet++ implementation and supporting source code used by the FaultNet models. This directory is based on a PyTorch implementation of PointNet/PointNet++ and retains its associated license information. - `requirements.txt`     Python packages required by the main FaultNet notebook. ## Installation Python 3 is required. To install the main dependencies, run: ```bash pip install -r requirements.txt ``` The supplied notebook loads the trained neural networks on the CPU by default. PyTorch can be configured separately for CUDA-enabled GPU execution if desired.   ## Citation If you use FaultNet or the materials in this archive, please cite the associated FaultNet publication and this Zenodo record. .. 10.5281/zenodo.22837108 ## Acknowledgments This work was supported by the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, Basic Energy Sciences (Award No. DE-SC0026319). ## License Please refer to the license information distributed with the relevant source-code components. Before public release, add the license selected for the FaultNet-specific code and trained models to the top-level archive.
items.title: FaultNet: Inferring Complex Fault Structures from Earthquake Hypocenter Distributions

items.summary: Direct numerical simulation (DNS) dataset of incompressible turbulent flow around a wall-mounted square cylinder, used as the training and evaluation data for Diff-SPORT, a diffusion-based framework for optimal sensor placement and sparse reconstruction of turbulent flows in urban environments (Vishwasrao et al., Nature Communications, in press; preprint arXiv:2506.00214). The simulation was performed with the open-source spectral-element code Nek5000 for an obstacle of width-to-height ratio b/h = 0.25 at a Reynolds number Re_h = 2000 based on the obstacle height h and the free-stream velocity. The computational domain spans -1 <= x/h <= 5, 0 <= y/h <= 2 and -1.5 <= z/h <= 1.5, and the velocity field is interpolated onto a uniform mesh. Snapshots are stored in convective time units with a sampling interval of 0.005. The simulation set-up and validation are documented in Martinez-Sanchez et al., J. Fluid Mech. 967, A1 (2023), https://doi.org/10.1017/jfm.2023.423. Files: U.mat, V.mat contain the streamwise, vertical velocity components, respectively, for a chunk of the three-dimensional DNS data (MATLAB v7.3 / HDF5 format).
items.title: DNS dataset of turbulent flow around a wall-mounted square cylinder (Re_h = 2000) for Diff-SPORT: Diffusion-based sensor placement optimization and reconstruction of turbulent flows in urban environments

items.summary: The article “The Image of Istanbul in the Russian Émigré, Soviet, and Modern Russian-Language Literature” explores various facets of the city’s image through the lens of the short stories and essays of the first wave of Russian émigrés’ literature, Soviet literary work of the 1920s-1930s, and contemporary Russian-language Azerbaijani prose. Literary works by Nadezhda Teffi Istanbul and the Sun (1921) and Gaito Gazdanov A Weak Heart (1927) explored in the article, focus on the émigré experience representing two most common ways of depicting Istanbul among the Russian émigré writers. Teffi neither succumbs to Orientalist fantasy nor reduces the city to a refugee misery, she supports both notions and considers Istanbul to be the city of exiles’ humiliation and artistic transcendence, whereas Gazdanov interprets the first center of Russian emigration more clearly and tragically, depicting it as a symbol of life without any moral support. Soviet literature portrays Istanbul in an entirely different manner. During the 1920s-1930s, the description of the East was ideologically justified as it implicitly prepared the ground for developing the internationalist theme of “the friendship of peoples”. Thus, Soviet writers focused mainly on the political, social, and cultural changes which occurred in Turkey during the 1920s, highlighting the country’s transformation from a historical enemy to potential ally. Sweet Salt of the Bosphorus (2008) by a contemporary Azerbaijani author Elchin Safarli who takes into account the artistic experience of Russian émigrés, creates a transcultural space that exhibits the following features of transliterary writing: the author’s specific bilingual linguistic consciousness, the reconstruction of an Azerbaijani worldview through the Russian language, an interlinguistic textual field, the foregrounding of the cultural integration of Russians in the East and an objective reconstruction by the writer, who belongs to the Eastern cultural code, of a “Russian” perspective on the world.
items.title: Image of Istanbul in the Russian émigré, Soviet, and modern Russian-language literature

items.summary: This dataset provides a curated and reproducible compilation of data used to analyze long-term trends in external-cause mortality in Ecuador from 1990 through 2024. The primary data sources are official mortality statistics and population estimates and projections published by Ecuador’s National Institute of Statistics and Censuses (Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censos, INEC). The dataset includes annual mortality counts and population-based indicators for major external-cause categories, including land transport injuries, other transport accidents and accidental injuries, suicide, homicide, events of undetermined intent, and other external causes. Where available, the data are organized by calendar year, sex, age or age group, geographic unit, ICD classification, and cause of death. Population denominators, crude mortality rates, confidence intervals, absolute and relative changes, mortality composition measures, sex-specific rate ratios, and variables used in the statistical analyses are documented separately from the original source data. The repository also contains information used to support the reproducibility of the associated scientific study, including analytical datasets, variable definitions, ICD harmonization information, population denominators, model-related variables, sensitivity-analysis data, quality-control documentation, data provenance, and records of differences identified between historical editions of INEC statistical tables. Hospital discharge datasets reviewed during data curation are documented at the variable and source level. Individual-level hospital discharge microdata are not included in the public dissemination package when their inclusion could create unnecessary privacy or re-identification risks. Original source information is kept distinct from derived variables and researcher-calculated indicators to preserve full provenance and auditability. The package follows FAIR data principles and includes machine-readable CSV files together with the original curated Excel database, a data dictionary, methodology documentation, provenance and transformation records, quality-control information, ethics and privacy considerations, citation metadata, licensing information, and version history. No missing values were imputed solely for publication, and no undocumented assumptions were used to generate unavailable data. Values for recent years should be interpreted according to the provisional or revised status indicated by the original INEC sources. This dataset is intended to support reproducibility, secondary epidemiological analyses, public health surveillance, methodological review, and research on injuries, violence, suicide, homicide, road traffic mortality, and other external causes of death in Ecuador.
items.title: Ecuador External-Cause Mortality, Population Denominators, and Reproducibility Dataset, 1990–2024

items.summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. items.summary: This technical note investigates whether operator-relative noncentrality can predict the relative empirical power of complementary localized scan statistics in correlated spectra. The motivating real-data benchmark compares BABAR and BESIII measurements of the e⁺e⁻ → π⁺π⁻ cross section in the ρ-resonance region on a common 5 MeV grid from 0.600 to 0.880 GeV. The real-data comparison remains negative, with no statistically supported localized shape tension identified. The methodological study compares a coherent-yield scan with a covariance-profiled shape scan and defines the frozen coordinate Θ = log(ES/EY), where ES and EY represent maximum local operator-accessible signal strengths. An archival confirmatory replication used 50,000 null calibration draws per covariance environment, 15,000 independent null-validation draws per environment, 1,440 signal/covariance conditions, and 576,000 injected pseudoexperiments. Θ predicted which scan had greater empirical power with pooled AUC 0.9820 and mean leave-one-covariance-environment-out AUC 0.9740; its correlation with the empirical power difference was 0.9185. Independent Type-I error estimates ranged from 0.0466 to 0.0540. The results support operator-relative noncentrality as a useful empirical coordinate for complementary globally calibrated scans within the tested benchmark. The underlying ingredients, including Gaussian noncentrality, covariance-weighted subspace detection, quadratic scanning, and Monte Carlo calibration, are established; the contribution is a reproducible computational synthesis and controlled characterization rather than a claim of a new general statistical law
items.title: Operator-Relative Noncentrality in Localized Correlated-Spectrum Scans: A BABAR–BESIII Benchmark

items.summary: Topic models, in particular Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), have been adapted to hyperspectral imagery (HSI) as a route to interpretable spectral mixtures: each spectral unit (canonically a pixel) becomes a document of quantised band-frequency tokens and the inferred topic-word distributions act as non-negative basis spectra. Yet the dominant evaluation criterion remains downstream classification accuracy, an accuracy-only view that is silent on whether the basis is reproducible, band-robust, calibrated, or actually outperforms standard linear baselines. We propose and instantiate a twelve-axis evaluation framework for LDA-style topic models on HSI that quantifies, on the same set of benchmarks: (F-1) classification macro-F1 compared across five method families (paired differences and a hierarchical Bayesian model), (F-2) topic-word coherence (c_v, c_NPMI, U-Mass), (F-3) seed stability for both LDA and two neural variants (ProdLDA, ETM), (F-4) capacity sensitivity across K in {4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16}, (F-5) band-mask robustness, (F-6) cross-method clustering agreement (LDA vs Felzenszwalb, SLIC, patches, pixels), (F-7) topic-label coupling via P(L | t) entropy and KL, (F-8) per-topic Hungarian-aligned identity tracking, (F-9) HIDSAG cross-preprocessing stability, (F-10) cross-scene topic transfer, (F-11) rate-distortion of the topic representation, and (F-12) external alignment of the topics with a spectral library and a method-rank cross-comparison. We apply the framework to six standard HSI benchmarks (Indian Pines, Salinas, Salinas-A, Pavia University, Kennedy Space Center, Botswana) and five subsets of the HIDSAG mineralogical database (GEOMET, MINERAL1, MINERAL2, GEOCHEM, PORPHYRY). The framework yields three findings that the accuracy-only view does not surface. First, on the labelled scenes the topic-routed soft classifier, which routes the raw spectrum to per-topic logistic experts, matches the raw-spectrum logistic baseline in macro-F1 (0.915 against 0.910, a paired difference of 0.005), while a logistic regression on the topic proportions theta alone trails the baseline by 0.325: the topics add an interpretable routing to the raw spectrum but do not replace it. Second, on Salinas-A under the SWIR-only band mask the paired ARI between canonical and masked dominant-topic maps reaches 0.766, while on Kennedy Space Center under every mask, and on Botswana under the SWIR mask, the same paired ARI collapses to approximately 0.01, separating scenes on which an interpretability claim is band-robust from scenes on which it is not. Third, the theta-only deficit holds on HIDSAG: over its nineteen mineralogical targets the topic-logistic classifier trails raw-logistic by 0.268 macro-F1 (lower on 18 of 19 targets), contrary to the prima-facie expectation that mineralogical mixtures favour topic decomposition over the raw spectrum. We release 3895 deterministic derived artefacts (449 MB), the builder source, the FastAPI backend, the React frontend, and a 109-endpoint test harness as a public, MIT-licensed reproducibility package. Code and derived artefacts: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_LDA_HSI . Interactive web application: https://lda-hsi.fasl-work.com . items.summary: Hashing Is Not Retrieval is a prospectively frozen three-arm evaluation of context accumulation in small-model multi-agent code cartography. It compares three ways for an orchestrator to hand work to a worker: 1. FULL HISTORY — retransmit prior worker outputs. 2. OPAQUE REF — replace the previous output with an unretrievable SHA-256 digest. 3. RETRIEVED — resolve the digest through a tenant-scoped content-addressed store and inject the recovered bytes. All arms receive identical source-derived evidence. The apparatus measures the exact message content sent to workers and records token counts, model and provider identifiers, generation IDs, usage, cost, retries, and retrieval proofs. A five-task gate preceded a fixed 50-task controlled benchmark, followed by a separate state-required evaluation across 24 deterministic fixtures and a five-scale Medusa case study. Key result: in the controlled benchmark, RETRIEVED reduced paired peak context by 38.3% relative to FULL HISTORY. The state-required follow-up shows that opaque references fail when state must be recovered, while verified retrieval preserves substantially more structural information. This is bounded-context evidence for automatic orchestrator-resolved state passing inside a specific two-worker code-cartography harness — not a universal claim about autonomous memory, long-context capability, or reasoning quality. The release includes the corrected author-identified preprint, executable apparatus, frozen results, task fixtures, telemetry, and verification instructions. Version 1.0.2 supplies the curated, verifier-passing reproducibility archive. It supersedes the uncurated archive from version 1.0.1 and includes the exact pinned apparatus, state-required fixtures, frozen results, and archive verifier. items.summary: This work studies whether internal rotation changes the longevity of source-free localized excitations in the reduced Enchan local time-rate field. The frozen scalar dynamics are S_tt = div[mu(D) grad S] - S with D = |grad S| and mu(D) = 1/(1 + D^(3/2)); no continuing external torque, centrifugal force, primitive matter source, or added rotational potential is used during the reported evolutions. Stage A supplies the non-rotating source-free baseline. Stage B1 initializes rotating phase-space states at omega = 4, 8, and 12 and evolves the extended runs to dimensionless time t = 100. Over 80 <= t <= 100, the mean localized-energy fractions are approximately 0.002207 for the non-rotating baseline and 0.006006, 0.149470, and 0.368846 for omega = 4, 8, and 12. The result is a graded rotation-associated longevity hierarchy: weak rotation gives little practical rescue, intermediate rotation substantially extends localization, and the strongest tested branch remains transient-localized through t = 100. Matched-energy near-zero-J_z controls provide a separate causality check and show that net canonical angular momentum alone is not a monotonic explanation of every late-time difference. Stage B2 separately tests spontaneous self-spin from exactly zero initial total angular momentum and finds no validated convergent counter-rotating branch in the tested scalar-only initial-data families. The ordered scan supports a physical formation picture in which a localized grain can move from weak rotational asymmetry through progressive spin-up into a strong-rotation long-lived branch. Time, space, and omega are dimensionless reduced-branch quantities; t = 100 is not assigned an SI duration in this work. The deposit contains the Version 1.0 manuscript PDF, a reproducibility ZIP with the publication source, code, selected archived numerical outputs, README, LICENSE, and SHA-256 integrity manifest. items.summary: This repository contains the data, documentation, and replication materials associated with the data paper on the  Cartulario de Santo Toribio de Liébana . The dataset provides a structured reconstruction of the documentary collection edited by Luis Sánchez Belda and converts the information contained in the cartulary into machine-readable research data. It covers 566 documentary acts and includes linked information on 576 payment or counter-performance elements, 603 place names, and 1,348 identified persons , together with a concordance between documentary numbering systems. The package preserves the documentary structure of the source while providing standardized variables suitable for quantitative and computational historical research. Particular attention is given to economic transactions. Payments and other forms of material counter-performance are recorded at the individual-component level rather than collapsed into a single transaction value. The data also distinguish operative contractual provisions from penalty clauses and other formulaic diplomatic material. Contains the materials required to reproduce and audit the construction of the dataset, including the structured datasets, extraction and coding documentation, variable definitions, provenance information, validation materials, and the code used for data processing and quality-control procedures. The replication workflow documents the transformation from the published documentary source to the final structured tables. It records corrections and normalization decisions while maintaining traceability to the underlying documentary act. The package is therefore intended not only to reproduce the published dataset but also to make individual coding decisions auditable. The dataset is designed for reuse in research on medieval economic history, property transactions, monastic institutions, historical geography, social networks, and computational approaches to diplomatic sources.

items.summary: Cyber threats directed against space systems (spanning orbital payloads, tracking and telemetry ground stations, downlinks, and upstream manufacturing supply chains) have evolved into acute operational hazards. Concurrently, national security and commercial defenders face an intelligence volume crisis where telemetry and vulnerability disclosures outpace human cognitive bandwidth. While autonomous multi-agent pipelines powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) offer scalable automation, they introduce severe epistemic liabilities: hallucination, source detachment, uncalibrated certainty, and susceptibility to indirect prompt injection. This paper presents Space-Cyber Brief Crew, a multi-agent cyber threat intelligence (CTI) architecture that automates space-domain intelligence synthesis under an explicit governance layer. Built on a decoupled CrewAI orchestration, the system routes structured reporting through a three-stage sequential pipeline (Collector, Analyst, Writer) governed by ten operational rules. Crucially, the architecture establishes a structural boundary between action capabilities and generative synthesis: downstream analysis agents operate in zero-tool sandboxes, restricting the execution attack surface by construction. We evaluate the framework against a tri-domain threat corpus spanning satellite imagery manipulation, ground industrial control systems (ICS), and global navigation satellite system (GNSS) spoofing. In our evaluation, the governed architecture eliminated identifier fabrication (from 23.3% to 0.0%), preserved 100% provenance retention, and neutralized indirect prompt injection attacks that succeeded in 80% of unconstrained baseline runs. Finally, we examine the institutional, regulatory, and oversight implications, establishing technical criteria for federal procurement and intelligence integration.

items.summary: A three-signal stopping rule for iterative LLM refinement derived from the Möbius theory stack: an equilibrium-distance surrogate d̂_R (RZGM meaning-equilibrium layer), an update-free-recurrence and diversity-collapse detector pair (Reflective Homeostasis Layer), and a hard reflection-depth cap (MUSE bounded reflection). Pre-registered study: 500 English prose-refinement tasks across ten domains, two generator models (Gemma4 12B-IT-QAT and 26B-A4B-IT-QAT), 8,000 generations, 999 blind position-swapped pairwise judgments. The governor cuts refinement tokens by 36.6% / 33.1% (bootstrap 95% CIs 33.6-39.5% / 30.3-35.9%) versus an always-eight-iterations baseline — 2.2-3.4x a naive convergence stop — at a measured quality cost reported at equal prominence: 38.0% / 36.6% of judged comparisons lost overall, a majority among actual interventions (61.1% / 59.0%), with measured cost almost perfectly collinear with output length. A full-data ablation shows the saturation signal is simultaneously the savings engine and the dominant cost source, yielding a measured two-point dial (10.0-11.5% savings at 8.2-11.8% loss rate with saturation disabled). Pre-release adversarial verification (four independent refuter passes) confirmed all headline statistics against the raw data and caught an inverted flagship anecdote: the corpus's two catastrophic degenerations (~50 verbatim paragraph repetitions) were selected once and avoided once by the governor, undetected in both cases — set-based trigram signals are structurally blind to within-output verbatim repetition. All tasks, rollouts, verdicts, audit votes, and analysis code are released in the companion repository. AI co-observer: Claude Fable 5 (Anthropic) — working method only; blind pairwise judging by Claude subagents under a position-swapped two-vote protocol; four independent adversarial refuter passes preceded release; the registered author is the human author alone. Version 1.1 (2026-09-19): adds (i) a proof-backed clarification that at window 3 the saturation condition is exactly “three identical consecutive non-rewrite change types” (the 0.70 threshold is inert there; companion note DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22842506), (ii) a pre-registered evaluation of a repetition-ratio guard as a fourth, roll-back signal — fires on both known collapses and 200/200 synthetic inflations, on 0 of 7,998 remaining published generations, 0 of 60 template expansions, and 0 of 960 held-out generations (verdict GO; pre-registration commit a89f722 precedes all evaluation data), and (iii) an expanded AI-authorship disclosure. All v1.0 numbers are unchanged. Version 1.2 (2026-09-19): adds (i) a length-stratified reanalysis of the 621 judged governor pairs (loss rate 92% where the early text is under 60% of the final length, 16.1% at near-equal length; 31 losses vs 4 wins at matched length, sign test p < 10 -5 — evidence of a content cost independent of length, not a decomposition of the headline cost), (ii) a held-out replication on 60 tasks authored after the fourth-signal pre-registration (token reduction 34.5% / 34.5%, loss rate 31.7% / 36.7%, main-study values inside the held-out intervals), and (iii) an online-intervention verification: an incremental governor reproduces all 1,000 published decisions (0 mismatches) and, run as a genuine online loop on the 60 held-out tasks with the 12B generator, generates 319 of 480 iterations with a stop distribution indistinguishable from the offline policy (permutation p = 0.46). All v1.0 and v1.1 numbers are unchanged. Version 1.3 (2026-09-19): adds a pre-registered length-matched re-judging (100 governor-loss pairs with early/final length ratio < 0.80; final text truncated at sentence boundaries to the early text's word count): the early text beats the length-matched final in 94/100 (loss 4%), and the full final beats its own truncation in 100/100.
